findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: Building Safety Act compliance has multiple unresolved issues with unclear timelines
findings.detail: Three building safety audit findings remain outstanding: tracking and reporting progress (status 'Partially Implemented'), building safety cases not current for High Rise Buildings (status 'TBC' with audit awaiting evidence), and lack of golden thread system in place (status unclear). Original deadlines were April 2026 and have been extended to TBC (to be confirmed), with no revised dates provided.
findings.matters: Building Safety Act compliance is statutory. Unresolved issues with unclear implementation dates represent legal and reputational risk, and the 'TBC' status suggests remediation planning is incomplete.
findings.figures: 3 Building Safety Act findings; original deadline April 2026 now TBC with no revised date confirmed
findings.quote: Building Safety Act – Housing – Follow up work: Building Safety Cases not current for all HRBs. Initially April 2026 now tbc. Management have advised completed, but internal audit are awaiting submission of evidence to support.

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: Control opinion was already at risk last year and has not materially improved
findings.detail: The CAE's conclusion is that controls are effective, but the historical comparison is telling: 2024/25 opinion was Reasonable 'but on the cusp of limited due to the number of lower assurance reports.' This year still has 2 limited assurance reports (housing complaints, repairs and adaptations, corporate property) and the opinion remains Reasonable, suggesting the control environment has not strengthened.
findings.matters: A control environment that was at the borderline of 'Limited' assurance last year and has not materially improved in the subsequent year suggests systemic issues are not being resolved.
findings.figures: 2024/25: Reasonable opinion 'on the cusp of limited'; 2025/26: Reasonable with 2 Limited assurance reports (originally 3, one resolved)
findings.quote: For information, this compares with 2024/25 where the overall opinion was Reasonable but on the cusp of limited due to the number of lower assurance reports.

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: Housing voids backlog remains above target with implementation date now extended to March 2027
findings.detail: The voids follow-up audit identified delays in pre and post-inspection completion of key fields. The original implementation date was May 2024, extended to July 2026, with the backlog issue itself now not expected to be resolved until March 2027. The paper notes voids turnaround has improved but 'remains above the target.'
findings.matters: Housing voids represent both capital asset utilization and rental income loss. A backlog extending to 2027 indicates operational/management control issues affecting a material revenue stream for a council with significant housing stock.
findings.figures: Original deadline May 2024 → July 2026 → March 2027 for voids backlog resolution
findings.quote: Voids turn around has been improved, but remains above the target.

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: 14 high-risk audit recommendations remain outstanding with repeated implementation date slippages
findings.detail: The council has 14 high-risk audit findings awaiting remediation, up from 6 in Q3. Multiple items have missed original deadlines and been pushed back repeatedly: voids backlog now extended to March 2027 (originally January 2025), data protection reporting now January 2027 (originally November 2025), building safety cases status unclear (originally April 2026). Several actions management claimed completed have been found by audit testing to still be in progress.
findings.matters: Outstanding high-risk audit findings indicate control weaknesses are not being fixed promptly, suggesting management capacity or priority issues. Repeated date slippages raise questions about the council's ability to execute remediation plans.
findings.figures: 14 high-risk recommendations outstanding (up from 6 in Q3); multiple remediation dates pushed back 6-14 months
findings.quote: There are 14 high risk recommendations that remain outstanding, which compares to 6 in quarter 3.

findings.headline: Social care and construction market failures narrowing supplier options and increasing costs
findings.detail: The Supplier/Market Failure risk (unmitigated score 24, mitigated 16) explicitly cites 'Recent examples of failure of construction firms, pressures and rising costs in social care market (adults and children's), private landlords leaving the market for temporary accommodation, limited market for repairs and maintenance contractors' alongside ongoing construction downturn limiting estate regeneration options.
findings.matters: Market tightness for social care suppliers and construction firms constrains the council's options and increases emergency repair/care costs; supplier failure examples suggest capacity is genuinely limited, not just pricing.
findings.figures: Supplier/Market Failure risk score: 24 unmitigated, 16 mitigated
findings.quote: Recent examples of failure of construction firms, pressures and rising costs in social care market (adults and children's), private landlords leaving the market for temporary accommodation, limited market for repairs and maintenance contractors and with the ongoing downturn in the construction industry limited market for estate regeneration projects.

findings.headline: Council taking direct operational control of stalled development sites previously managed through council-owned vehicles
findings.detail: The council states 'Work on the stalled BL / BLRP sites now been reviewed and will be led by the Council,' appearing under the Supplier/Market Failure risk. This indicates council-owned development vehicles have stalled projects that the council is reassuming control of, suggesting those vehicles were unable to deliver.
findings.matters: Stalled development projects represent capital tied up with uncertain return; the transfer from arm's-length vehicles to direct council management signals those vehicles underperformed and the council must absorb delivery risk.
findings.figures: Number and value of sites not disclosed
findings.quote: Work on the stalled BL / BLRP sites now been reviewed and will be led by the Council.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs forcing service redesign ahead of 2026/27
findings.detail: The council identifies 'Cost pressures with the homelessness service (TA)' as part of the Financial Resilience risk, with planned 'Review of programme and priorities ahead of 2026/27' that implies service reductions or refocusing. The mitigation strategy includes 'Housing Demand Programme to mitigation financial pressures,' suggesting anticipated budget constraints are driving operational change.
findings.matters: Homelessness TA is often the fastest-growing and least controllable spend; planned service model changes indicate the council expects to constrain this budget through redesign rather than volume reductions.
findings.figures: Not quantified; described as significant cost pressure driving 2026/27 programme review
findings.quote: Cost pressures with the homelessness service (TA). Review of programme and priorities ahead of 2026/27– to refocus effort and resources.

findings.headline: Council's capital financing requirement of £1,043m exceeds external borrowing by £201m, with the gap covered by internal borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement stands at £1,043.462m against actual borrowing of £841.973m. The council explicitly confirms: "borrowing requirements are financed through both external and internal borrowing, although no external borrowing was raised during the financial year". This £201.489m gap is being filled through reserves.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing (cash use) is a finite strategy; as reserves deplete, the council will need to raise external borrowing, potentially at rates higher than locked-in borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £1,043.462m, external borrowing £841.973m, creating a £201.489m internal borrowing gap
findings.quote: The council's actual borrowing stood at £841.973m which is below the CFR of £1,043.462m. The council's borrowing requirements are financed through both external and internal borrowing, although no external borrowing was raised during the financial year.

findings.headline: Investment balances fell 30% as council funded capital expenditure from cash reserves rather than external borrowing.
findings.detail: Council investment balances declined from £417.056m to £290.109m (£126.947m decrease) over the year. The paper explicitly links this to capital funding: "cash balances are used to fund capital expenditure". This is a significant drawdown of the council's liquid reserves in a single year.
findings.matters: Cash reserves are finite; capital funded from reserves rather than sustainable borrowing will eventually deplete working capital or force external borrowing.
findings.figures: Investment balance £417.056m (31 March 2025) to £290.109m (31 March 2026), a decrease of £126.947m or 30.4%
findings.quote: There is a decrease in the investment balance from £417.056m at 31 March 2025 to £290.109m at 31 March 2026 as cash balances are used to fund capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Council tax and business rates collection both fell 1.12% short of target, leaving £4.999m uncollected in-year.
findings.detail: Council tax in-year collection was 95.88%, missing the 97% target by £2.933m. Business rates collection was 95.38%, missing the 96.5% target by £2.066m. Council tax collection deteriorated 0.97% against the prior year, suggesting collection pressure is worsening.
findings.matters: Collection shortfalls reduce in-year income and require management action or service cuts to stay in balance. Deteriorating collection is a leading indicator of resident and business financial stress within the district.
findings.figures: Council tax shortfall £2.933m (1.12% below 97% target). Business rates shortfall £2.066m (1.12% below 96.5% target). Combined £4.999m uncollected.
findings.quote: Council tax in-year collection was 95.88% which is 1.12% behind the target collection profile (97%) which equates to £2.933m.

findings.headline: Council is deliberately building general fund reserves to £21.252m (6.5% of budget) to manage financial uncertainty, while noting other London boroughs' balances are reducing.
findings.detail: The General Fund balance was increased by the 2025/26 underspend to £21.252m. The S151 Officer's March 2026 risk assessment set the adequate range at £17.5m–£25m. The paper notes the council is now 'increasing its balances at a time where other London boroughs' balances are reducing,' suggesting Ealing faces sharper financial stress than its peers.
findings.matters: A council building reserves while peers draw them down signals it expects sustained financial stress. The explicit comparison (other boroughs reducing balances) suggests Ealing's underlying pressures exceed the sector average.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £21.252m at 31 March 2026 (6.5% of net budget requirement). Opening balance £20.472m. S151 Officer adequate range £17.5m–£25m.
findings.quote: The council is increasing its balances at a time where other London boroughs' balances are reducing.

findings.headline: £18.366m High Needs Block DSG deficit persists despite statutory reforms; new stability grant covers only 90% of accumulated deficit.
findings.detail: The council reports a ring-fenced DSG deficit of £18.366m on the High Needs Block. The paper notes that 'Around 90% of High Need Block funding is committed to meeting statutory duties for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), limiting flexibility to manage in-year pressures.' Although a new High Needs Stability Grant will fund 90% of the historic deficit from 2026/27, the paper warns that reform programmes 'will not address the current level of financial pressure in the short term.'
findings.matters: This is a ring-fenced deficit that cannot be subsidised from the General Fund. It must be cleared from DSG income. The partial grant leaves 10% of the historic deficit unfunded and does not resolve ongoing pressure.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit £18.519m (High Needs £18.366m, Schools Block £0.153m). High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of the High Needs deficit from 2026/27.
findings.quote: Around 90% of High Need Block funding is committed to meeting statutory duties for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), limiting flexibility to manage in-year pressures.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £7.519m driven by housing benefit subsidy shortfall, a structural pressure reflecting national housing shortage.
findings.detail: Housing & Environment overspent by £7.519m on temporary accommodation, mainly due to 'housing benefit subsidy shortfall, other temporary accommodation net costs and an increase in the bad debt provision.' This is a demand-driven pressure reflecting the national shortage of permanent housing stock and reflects policy constraints (council cannot refuse homeless duties).
findings.matters: This is a structural pressure Ealing cannot control, rooted in national housing policy and shortage. It will persist and likely grow, representing a fixed cost drain on the budget.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation overspend £7.519m within £1.993m Housing & Environment underspend.
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation overspend of £7.519m mainly relates to housing benefit subsidy shortfall, other temporary accommodation net costs and an increase in the bad debt provision.

findings.headline: Paper warns explicitly that demand-led cost and volume pressures will persist into 2026/27 despite budget growth, signalling sustained financial stress ahead.
findings.detail: The outturn summary states that although an underspend was delivered, 'significant overspends were experienced, especially in demand led services. Whilst budget growth has been included in many of these budgets for 2026/27, there remain significant ongoing risks of rising costs, demand and complexity of that demand that will need to be managed to achieve a balanced outturn for 2026/27.' This is an explicit admission the structural problem will not be solved.
findings.matters: The council is signalling it expects 2026/27 to remain difficult. Growth already allocated may not be sufficient, suggesting a budget-setting challenge ahead and potential further deficits or reserve draws.
findings.figures: No 2026/27 figures provided; forward-looking warning only.
findings.quote: Whilst budget growth has been included in many of these budgets for 2026/27, there remain significant ongoing risks of rising costs, demand and complexity of that demand that will need to be managed to achieve a balanced outturn for 2026/27.

findings.headline: The council's £0.780m underspend is entirely dependent on one-off interest income and capital delays; remove these and the position is £5m overspent.
findings.detail: The reported underspend is 'principally due to the interest earned on cash balances... due to interest rates remaining higher for longer than anticipated and delays in the capital programme.' Quarter 3 forecast showed a £5.023m overspend before these temporary benefits. Services overspent by £13.540m but this was masked by £13.684m of corporate underspends (interest income). This is not sustainable.
findings.matters: The headline outturn is misleading. The actual service position is structurally overspent by £5m+. When interest rates normalise and capital catch-up spending occurs, the council's true financial position will be exposed.
findings.figures: Outturn underspend £0.780m. Services net overspend £13.540m. Corporate budget underspend £13.684m (interest-driven). Q3 forecast showed £5.023m overspend.
findings.quote: The additional interest, and other one-off or time-limited corporate budgets and contingencies, enabled the council to off-set service overspends and contribute to general balances by £0.780m (0.24% of the net revenue budget).

findings.headline: £9.027m overspend in adults social care and £6.968m in children's services despite budget growth, driven by placement cost inflation the council cannot control.
findings.detail: Adults & Public Health overspent by £9.027m, primarily due to placement pressures with a gross placements overspend of £17.106m. Children's & Schools overspent by £6.968m, with residential care alone costing £4.828m over budget. The paper notes average weekly cost increases of £2.9m in children's residential care since 2024/25, reflecting market-rate inflation rather than volume.
findings.matters: These are structural pressures driven by market costs and statutory duties, not controllable by the council. Even with allocated growth, costs are running ahead. This pattern is forecast to continue into 2026/27.
findings.figures: Adults overspend £9.027m. Children's overspend £6.968m. Placement gross overspend £17.106m. Children's residential care average weekly increase £2.9m since 2024/25.
findings.quote: Despite that growth, these severe pressures remain and have resulted in overspends across these areas.

findings.headline: Business rates safety net falls from 100% to 92.5% after 2026/27, exposing council to collection shortfalls
findings.detail: Government protection on business rates falls from 100% safety net in 2026/27 to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% from 2028/29 onwards. The council's forecast collection of £236.277m is vulnerable to local economic conditions affecting business valuations and occupancy. Any shortfall below the declining safety net threshold directly reduces the council's available funding. The council acknowledges this risk 'will need to be closely monitored during the year.'
findings.matters: Business rates income is volatile. The declining government protection means economic downturns affecting the borough's business base will reduce council income without equivalent compensation, directly threatening financial sustainability in a weaker economy.
findings.figures: 100% safety net 2026/27, declining to 97% (2027/28) and 92.5% (2028/29); £236.277m total collection forecast, £70.883m retained by council, £0.238m safety net payment expected 2026/27
findings.quote: The Safety Net threshold will gradually revert to 92.5% for most authorities over the settlement period. Therefore, based on current estimates the council will expect to receive a safety net payment of £0.238m in 2026/27. This safety net payment will ensure the council received the government assumed business rates baseline in 2026/27, although there will be risks to the baseline income in future years should the council's business rates base reduce.

findings.headline: High Needs Block pressure forcing continued 0.5% transfer from mainstream schools funding
findings.detail: The council continues the 0.5% transfer from Schools Block to High Needs Block in 2026/27 (£1.712m) as a mitigation for SEND funding shortfall. The document states the council is 'currently faced with a projected pressure which is being partially mitigated through revised management actions'—the language 'currently' and 'partially' indicates the underlying pressure remains unresolved and is merely being managed through inter-block transfers that reduce mainstream schools' funding.
findings.matters: This reveals an ongoing structural mismatch between SEND demand and SEND funding that the council is managing through transfers from mainstream schools. If this pressure escalates or the transfer cannot continue, it creates risk to both SEND provision and schools' operational budgets.
findings.figures: 0.5% transfer (£1.712m) from Schools Block to High Needs Block in 2026/27, described as continuation of previous years' transfers
findings.quote: The council is currently faced with a projected pressure which is being partially mitigated through revised management actions, including the continued 0.5% transfer from the SB in 2026/27

findings.headline: £18.6m combined pressure in children's and adults' social care pressures continuing through 2029
findings.detail: Children's Services faces £12.796m pressure in 2026/27 (forecast £3.664m in 2027/28, £1.487m in 2028/29), and Adult Social Care £6.539m (forecast £4.549m in 2027/28, £3.649m in 2028/29). Temporary accommodation adds a further £5.824m pressure in 2026/27. The council notes these challenges are 'especially pronounced for the council as a London borough' due to housing costs and demographic factors. These are demand-driven pressures, not efficiency issues, and the council projects they will persist.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures in statutory services (social care, homelessness) cannot be easily controlled through efficiency savings alone, creating ongoing budget risk and vulnerability to in-year overspends.
findings.quote: Local authorities continue to face significant demand and market pressures, particularly in adults' and children's social care and in the provision of temporary accommodation for homeless households. These challenges are especially pronounced for the council as a London borough.

findings.headline: Ring-fenced schools deficit tripling: DSG account forecast to reach £17.537m by end 2025/26
findings.detail: Ealing's Dedicated Schools Grant account (ring-fenced) held a £5.641m deficit at end 2024/25 and is forecasting £17.537m by Q3 2025/26. This is driven primarily by High Needs Block pressures in special educational needs. Nationally, DSG deficits are forecast to reach £4.6bn by March 2026, up from £3.2bn in March 2025. While the government will write off 90% of the historic deficit in 2026/27, the council still faces ongoing structural SEND funding pressure.
findings.matters: The rapid growth of the DSG deficit signals the current SEND funding model is unsustainable, constraining future flexibility in education spending and indicating a structural problem in meeting statutory special needs duties.
findings.figures: £5.641m DSG deficit end 2024/25; £17.537m forecast Q3 2025/26; national estimate £3.2bn (March 2025) rising to £4.6bn (March 2026)
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25 the council held a net deficit balance of £5.641m on its DSG account. At the end of Quarter 3 of 2025/26, the council is forecasting a net deficit of £17.537m for the year

findings.headline: Budget path unsustainable: £7.893m deficit forecast by 2029/30 with no mitigation plan
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is balanced, but projected budgets show a cumulative deficit of £7.893m by 2029/30. The council explicitly acknowledges this requires 'additional funding and reduced service costs, and/ or additional income to achieve a sustainable budget in the medium-term through to 2030.' No mitigation strategy or solution has yet been identified for this structural imbalance, creating a medium-term refinancing risk.
findings.matters: A lender assessing refinancing risk in 3-4 years needs to understand the council faces difficult decisions on funding or service levels, and current trends are unsustainable without intervention.
findings.figures: £7.893m cumulative deficit by 2029/30
findings.quote: The projected budgets for the next three years show a cumulative deficit of £7.893m by 2029/30. This highlights the need for additional funding and reduced service costs, and/ or additional income to achieve a sustainable budget in the medium-term through to 2030.

findings.headline: Asset disposal timing and value is highly volatile and shortfalls must be met from increased borrowing
findings.detail: Capital receipts from asset sales are identified as the most unpredictable element of capital funding. If disposals underperform against forecast, the council must increase borrowing to cover the gap, up to the agreed Authorised Borrowing Limit. Given the council's stated reluctance to borrow, receipt shortfalls could force difficult trade-offs.
findings.matters: Asset sales volatility creates cash flow and funding risk. A poorly performing property market or delays in disposals would force additional borrowing, directly conflicting with the stated policy of minimising new debt.
findings.figures: Capital receipts planned: £24.059m (General Fund) and £119.657m (HRA) over 2025/26-2030/31
findings.quote: The timing and value of asset sales is the most volatile element of funding. As a result, the Strategic Director, Resources closely monitors progress on asset disposals. Any in-year shortfalls against forecasts will need to be met from increased borrowing, up to the 'Authorised Borrowing Limit' which is agreed annually as part of the Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Delivery of the council's climate programme is highly dependent on securing competitive government and external grants with no guarantee of success
findings.detail: The council's ability to fund climate investments relies heavily on external funding sources that are competitive and uncertain. Officer time is spent preparing bids to government funding pots. If funding bids fail, the council's climate targets and capital programme commitments may not be deliverable.
findings.matters: Dependence on external grant funding creates delivery risk. A failure to secure expected grants would force either unplanned borrowing (contrary to stated policy) or deferral of committed projects, affecting service and stakeholder confidence.
findings.figures: £14.1m approved capital investment in Greener Ealing Limited includes leasing/vehicles; 150 bike hangars programme continues; Young Adults Centre opened spring 2025
findings.quote: Currently, delivery of the council's climate programme is highly contingent on external funding sources, often originating from government, to fund climate investments, such as schemes relating to corporate and domestic energy efficiency and retrofit. Officer time is required to prepare bids for these funding pots, which are usually competitive, thereby providing no guarantee of success.

findings.headline: The council's medium-term financial strategy shows a balanced budget for 2026/27 but has an unresolved budget gap in future years
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is balanced, the MTFS projects a budget gap beyond that period that will require action. The document does not specify the size of this gap or when it emerges, leaving uncertainty about the severity of future financial pressure.
findings.matters: This signals that the council's financial position will come under pressure in coming years, which affects its ability to service debt, fund capital investment, and maintain services. It may be a precursor to savings plans or service changes.
findings.figures: Capital programme total 2025/26-2030/31: £1,377.78m; budget balanced in 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The council's MTFS shows a balanced budget for 2026/27. However there is a budget gap in future years that will need to be addressed.

findings.headline: Broadway Living Registered Provider's business model is under review with no agreed path forward yet
findings.detail: Following the contractor insolvency and inability to deliver the original plan, BLRP's Managing Director and Board are reviewing options for a viable alternative business plan with external advisers (Campbell Tickell). Proposals are being reviewed for 2025/26 but have not yet been finalised. The impact on the Capital Strategy will be determined once proposals are agreed.
findings.matters: Until BLRP's future model is resolved, there is uncertainty about what capital will be needed, how much council loan funding will be deployed, and what revenue return the council can expect from this investment.
findings.figures: Original plan: 1,471 new homes; current status: 2 schemes complete, 1 at completion, 4 paused
findings.quote: The BLRP Managing Director and Board are now reviewing options for a viable business plan, advised by Campbell Tickell, and proposals are currently being reviewed for the financial year 2025/26. Once those proposals are considered, the impact on the Capital Strategy and Programme will be considered.

findings.headline: From 2026/27, new capital schemes will not be funded from borrowing because the council has high historic debt
findings.detail: The council has explicitly adopted a constraint on its capital programme to avoid further borrowing. This reflects a recognition that existing debt levels are limiting. Any new capital investment will need to come from external grants, capital receipts, or revenue contributions rather than prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's current debt capacity and constraints. An explicit policy against new borrowing signals fiscal stress and limits the council's future investment flexibility.
findings.figures: £1,456.205m capital programme over 2025/26 to 2030/31; council's MTFS shows a balanced budget for 2026/27 but a budget gap in future years
findings.quote: capital schemes will not be undertaken unless they can be funded from sources other than borrowing, as the council has a high level of historic debt

findings.paper_title: 4.3. Appendix 3 LBE Pension Fund_Forvis Mazars ACR 2024-25
findings.headline: Fund does not perform full user access reviews; only approver-level access reviewed, creating risk of unauthorized journal posting
findings.detail: The audit identified a control deficiency: the fund does not perform a full user access review covering all staff. Only those with approver access were reviewed for appropriateness of system access to Agresso BWO. This gap creates potential for fraudulent journals to be posted. Management is implementing full role reviews as part of Business World migration scheduled for August 2026.
findings.matters: User access controls are fundamental to preventing unauthorized or fraudulent transactions in financial systems; gaps in access reviews indicate control environment weakness affecting the council's financial controls
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Fund does not perform a full user access review where appropriateness of access for application user base is considered. We noted that a user access review was not carried out for all staff but only those with approver access.

findings.paper_title: 4.3. Appendix 3 LBE Pension Fund_Forvis Mazars ACR 2024-25
findings.headline: Fund previously misclassified a major investment (Federated Hermes) by over £35 million between fair value hierarchy levels, now corrected
findings.detail: In prior years 2022/23 and 2023/24, the Federated Hermes investment was incorrectly classified as level 2 when it should have been level 3, requiring corrections of £35.6 million and £33 million respectively. This significant deficiency has been resolved after management performed a thorough review of all investment classifications.
findings.matters: Shows the fund has had recurring investment classification governance issues; while now fixed, indicates historical weakness in valuation controls that affect the pension liability measurement
findings.figures: £35,625k correction (2022/23), £32,968k correction (2023/24)
findings.quote: Classification of investments within the fair value hierarchy. We noted that 'Federated Hermes' investment asset was classified as level 2 in both 2022/23 and 2023/24 but should have been level 3. This resulted in a classification adjustment of £35,625k in 2022/23 and £32,968k in 2023/24

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee review and report to Council final draft to AC
findings.headline: Risk management strategy last formally approved February 2022, unchanged for over 3.5 years.
findings.detail: The Audit Committee receives regular risk reports and reviews the strategy, but the strategy itself was last formally approved in February 2022. No update or approval of a refreshed strategy is mentioned in this 2025/26 review despite the extended period.
findings.matters: A static risk strategy over 3.5 years is unlikely to reflect changes in council operations, strategic priorities, or emerging risks. Lenders assess governance quality partly through the currency of risk frameworks.
findings.figures: February 2022
findings.quote: A risk report is received at each meeting. This includes a regular review of the strategy (last approved February 2022).

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee review and report to Council final draft to AC
findings.headline: External auditor issued a disclaimed opinion in 2024/25, removing audit assurance on financial statements.
findings.detail: The paper states the external auditor provided a disclaimed opinion during 2024/25. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not form an opinion on whether the financial statements are true and fair—the most serious audit outcome. The paper attributes this to national audit backlog delays, though notes the backlog has been 'largely addressed.'
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion eliminates external assurance on financial statement accuracy. This removes a primary control that lenders rely on to verify reported financial position, even if the underlying cause is temporary.
findings.quote: During 2024/25 the audit backlog was largely addressed, although the external auditor provided a disclaimed opinion in line with the national delays and government solution to address audit backlogs.
